newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian politics drives many to wilderness.
newsitem.headline: Algerian politics drives many to wilderness.

text.p: From the heady days of its race to democracy, back in the now blood-shrouded mists of 1990, Algeria is facing change that is expected to drive most of its political parties into the wilderness.
Politicians and political analysts say the existing 69 parties, many tiny and inactive, will shrink to around four, the rest driven by laws passed this week to extinction.
The most powerful opposition party from the last, aborted, general election, the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), will have no voice, its leaders still jailed and itself outlawed.

Algerian President Liamine Zeroual said three years ago the nation of 29 million people was near disaster through political and ideological splits -- the mushroom result of reform when any 15 people could form a party, and get state backing.
He sees the new laws, banning parties based on Islam, language, sex or regions, plus a proportional representation system of voting, as the way toward democracy and stability.
And an end to violence. Not everyone agrees.

"It is a closed political ring dominated by the military. Unfortunately, the government has chosen a destructive policy which results in subjugating completely civil society," says Hocine Ait Ahmed, leader of the Socialist Forces Front (FFS).
His party came second in the first round of the aborted 1992 poll -- way behind the FIS which needed only 28 more seats from run-off voting to win an absolute parliamentary majority.

The path to change is strewn with the bodies of about 60,000 people, killed in the struggle between the authorities and hardline Islamic fundamentalists who say the scrapped 1992 election was proof that power can come only from the gun.

Zeroual's supporters say his bid to lay the foundations for a "new national political order" will take Algeria to stability and help the national elite focus on its fundamental needs: development and social justice.
Noureddine Boukrouh, head of the moderate Islamist-leaning Algerian Renewal Party, said Zeroual's drive to restructure the political spectrum will wipe out "political parasitism".

"It will clear out the political climates. Only the true political parties will find their places. I mean by true political parties those which have comprehensive programmes answering our people needs to get out of economic underdevelopment," said Boukrouh in a recent interview.
THREE PRONGED STRATEGY

Political analysts say the government has a three-pronged strategy to realise its plan: tightened legislation; the authorities attempts to set up its own political party, plunged into disarray by the killing of leader-designate Abdelhak Benhamouda last month; and a president with paramount powers.

The government-appointed Transitional National Council (CNT), a quasi-parliament, this week voted party and election laws that will sweep away at least 60 of the 69 registered political parties, analysts say.
The 44-article party law says any political party has to prove it has support in at least 25 of Algeria's 48 provinces.
"The number of members at each wilaya (province) must be at least equal to 100," the law stipulates. And at least 20 party leaders said this month the law sounded their party's closure.
The law also bars politicians from campaigning on the basis of the Moslem faith, the Arab and Berber languages, gender issues or regional differences.
Berber activists fear that will hinder their cause to see their language recognised as an official one alongside Arabic.

They also fear that berber-dominated parties, the Rally of Culture and Democracy (RCD) as well as Ait Ahmed's FFS might be threatened, as the two groups are mainly represented in three northeastern regions of Tizi-ouzou, Bejaia and Bouira.

While the law gives both legal fundamentalist Islamist parties, Hamas and Nahda, two months to change their manifestos, Moslem rebels added the law to their ideological offensive against Zeroual's government.

"The law bares the tyrants' designs to put again Islam on the shelf by banning lovers of God to heighten the faith's sacred cause," said Algeria's ruthless Armed Islamic Group (GIA) in a statement this month.
GOVERNMENT STILL FEARS FUNDAMENTALIST REVIVAL
Algeria's leaders are taking no chances on a return to the political map of the early 1990s.

"This time the authorities are hammering the point home: the laxity of the end of the 1980s is over for ever," said analyst Aouimer Ammar, refering to the leadership which presided over the ill-fated multiparty democracy debut in 1989.
Political sources say the authorities are still haunted by what a Zeroual adviser called "the 1992 nightmare" and fear Hamas winning massively in elections promised by July 1997.
Hamas leader Mahfoud Nahnah won one-third of the vote in the 1995 presidential poll, behind the victor Zeroual.
"It is clear that the election law aims at preventing any party snatching a majority in parliament in the next election," said one political source.
Most analysts forecast several parties to merge and others to sink into oblivion.

"An overall picture of the political situation may be drawn around four main political currents: a moderate Islamist movement, a left-wing pole grouped around FFS, a nationalist centrist party around the National Liberation Front (FLN) and a radical hawkish anti-Islamist movement in which (former prime minister) Redha Malek and (RCD leader) Said Saadi are the main proponents," said analyst Ammar.
